15.title: forty days
15.hook: forty days; giving something up is a way of paying attention
15.howItsDone: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday, fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, abstain from meat on Fridays in Lent, and take on prayer, fasting and almsgiving for the forty days before Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Our Father, and the family word at the start of it. Your line was: not a stranger. Who did you treat like family? Day fifteen.

One Wednesday every year, usually in February or March, you might notice something strange at work. The woman at the next desk has a smudge of black on her forehead. Then the guy at the coffee shop. Then a kid on the train. Someone reaches over to tell them they've got dirt on their face, and they smile and say: it's Ash Wednesday. For the next six weeks, your Catholic friends might be off chocolate, or off social media, or eating fish on Fridays. It looks like a diet with a religious excuse. It isn't about the chocolate at all. Today, forty days of paying attention.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `IT'S ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `IT ISN'T ABOUT THE CHOCOLATE.`

segments.voice: Lent is the season of forty days before Easter. The English word is old: it comes from an Old English word for spring, when the days lengthen. And forty is one of the Bible's favorite numbers for a time of testing. Noah's rain falls forty days. Moses stays on the mountain forty days. Israel wanders forty years. And in Matthew's Gospel, right after his baptism, Jesus goes into the desert, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry." Lent is Catholics walking alongside those forty days. It starts with the ashes. The priest or minister marks a cross on the forehead with ash, and may say words from Genesis: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." It sounds grim. Catholics hear it as honest. You won't be here forever, so what are you doing with the time? Then come the three old practices, the same three Jesus names in the Sermon on the Mount: prayer, fasting, and giving to the poor. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and skip meat on Fridays. Many give something up for the whole season. Here's the idea underneath. When you give up something small, every time you reach for it, you notice. The reach becomes a reminder. The empty space where the chocolate used to be becomes a little room for prayer, or for someone else. Less, on purpose. Many Catholics also add something: a daily walk, a visit to someone lonely, money set aside for the hungry. And the forty days only make sense because of where they end: Easter morning.
screen: `LENT — THE DAYS LENGTHEN.` · `FORTY: NOAH, MOSES, THE DESERT.` · `DUST THOU ART.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · then, large: `THE REACH BECOMES A REMINDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Think of one small thing you reach for without thinking. Your phone. A snack. A complaint. Don't give it up yet. Just picture yourself reaching for it, and stopping, hand in the air. What would you notice in that moment instead? Stay there, breathing slowly, in the pause before the reach. If you pray, you can offer that pause to God. The bell holds the time.
Lent. Forty days before Easter, of prayer, fasting and giving, where less becomes a way of paying attention. Fifteenth word.
Your line: less, on purpose. Today, skip one small thing you'd usually reach for, and each time you miss it, let it remind you of someone. Day fifteen.

16.title: the women went first
16.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Easter with the Easter Vigil on Saturday night and Mass on Easter Sunday, and keep the Easter season for fifty days, until Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lent: forty days, and the ashes. Your line was: less, on purpose. What did you reach for and skip? Today, where the forty days end. Day sixteen.

It's still dark. A Sunday morning in Jerusalem, two days after the execution. The men who followed Jesus are hiding. And a few women are walking to a tomb cut in the rock, carrying spices to anoint a body. That's what you did for someone you loved. On the way, they realize they have a problem. There's a huge stone rolled across the entrance, far too heavy for them. In Mark's Gospel, they ask each other: "Who shall roll us back the stone from the door of the sepulchre?" They go anyway. They don't have a plan. They just go. Today, the morning the whole Catholic year is built around.
screen: `STILL DARK. A SUNDAY.` → `THE MEN ARE HIDING.` → `WHO WILL ROLL BACK THE STONE?`

segments.voice: When they get there, the stone is already rolled away. The tomb is empty. In Luke's Gospel, two men in shining clothes ask them why they're looking for the living among the dead, and say, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "He is not here, but is risen." Every Gospel tells it a little differently: how many women, how many angels, who sees what first. But all four agree on one thing that would have surprised anyone at the time: women were the first witnesses. In that world, a woman's testimony often counted for less in court. If you were inventing a story to convince people, you probably wouldn't write it that way. And Luke admits the men didn't believe them at first. The women's words, he says, seemed like idle tales. In John's Gospel, Mary Magdalene stays behind at the tomb, crying, and meets the risen Jesus himself, and doesn't recognize him until he says her name. Then he sends her to tell the others. That's why the Church has long called her the apostle to the apostles: the one sent to the ones who would be sent. Catholics believe the resurrection is the center of everything: that Jesus truly rose from the dead, and that death doesn't get the last word. That's why every Sunday is a little Easter, from day thirteen. Easter itself isn't just one day. It's a season of fifty days, longer than Lent. In most languages the feast's name comes from Pascha, the Passover. English is one of the few that says Easter. And look at the order of that morning. The women were worrying about the stone the whole way there. By the time they arrived, it had already been moved.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Think of one stone you're worried about. Something ahead of you that feels too heavy to move: a conversation, a bill, a diagnosis, a decision. Picture yourself walking toward it anyway, like the women did, without a plan. Breathe slowly as you walk. You don't have to solve it. Just keep walking. If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Easter. The feast of the resurrection, the empty tomb, and the women who were sent to tell. Sixteenth word.
Your line: the stone is already moved. Today, take one step toward the thing you've been dreading, and see if it's as heavy as you thought. Day sixteen.

17.title: why Catholics say "presence"
17.howItsDone: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering a church, and many spend quiet time in prayer before it, a practice called adoration.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Easter: the women walking in the dark, and the empty tomb. Your line was: the stone is already moved. Did you take one step? Day seventeen.

Watch Catholics walk into an empty church on a Tuesday afternoon. No Mass, no music, nobody at the front. And yet, before they slide into a pew, many of them drop to one knee, facing a small box of gold or wood near the altar, with the little red lamp burning beside it. You met that lamp on day nine. Why kneel to a box in an empty room? Because Catholics don't think the room is empty. On day five we saw the bread and wine at Mass, and promised to come back to the big claim. Today we do. Why Catholics say presence.
screen: `AN EMPTY CHURCH ON A TUESDAY.` → `ONE KNEE, FACING A SMALL BOX.` → `NOT AN EMPTY ROOM.`

segments.voice: The word is Eucharist, from the Greek eucharistia, which means thanksgiving. At the Last Supper, the Gospels say, Jesus took bread and gave thanks. So the whole meal is named after a thank-you. Here's the claim. Catholics believe that when the priest says the words of the Last Supper at Mass, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. They still look, taste and feel like bread and wine. But what they are, underneath, has changed. The Church calls this transubstantiation, a word it formally used starting in the Middle Ages, and it calls the result the real presence. Not a symbol of him. Him. Catholics point to John's Gospel, where Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "I am the living bread which came down from heaven." And then even more bluntly: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." John says many followers found this too hard and walked away. Jesus didn't soften it. He let them go. That's the backbone of Catholic belief here. And after Mass, the consecrated bread that's left over is kept in that small box, the tabernacle. That's why the red lamp burns, and why people kneel as they come in. They believe he's there. Christians understand this differently, and it's worth saying plainly. Orthodox Christians also believe in a real presence, usually without using that Latin word. Lutherans speak of a real presence too, in their own terms. Many other Protestants understand communion as a memorial and a sign. At the end of Matthew's Gospel, Jesus promises: "I am with you all days." Catholics hear the tabernacle as that promise, kept in a room. He stayed.
screen: `EUCHARISTIA — THANKSGIVING.` · `STILL LOOKS LIKE BREAD.` · `I AM THE LIVING BREAD.` · `THE TABERNACLE AND THE LAMP.` · then, large: `HE STAYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Think of a time someone simply stayed with you. They didn't fix anything. They sat in the hospital waiting room, or on the end of your bed, or on the phone while you cried. Remember what it felt like not to be alone. Let that feeling fill the whole time. If you pray, you can rest in the thought that you're not alone now, either. The bell holds the time.
The Eucharist. Thanksgiving: the bread and wine Catholics believe become Christ's body and blood, his real presence. Seventeenth word.
Your line: he stayed. Today, stay with someone a little longer than you need to: on the phone, at the table, at the door. Day seventeen.

18.title: one, holy, catholic
18.hook: one, holy, catholic — the small-c word means universal
18.tomorrow: the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship
18.howItsDone: Every Sunday at Mass, Catholics profess the Nicene Creed, including belief in "one, holy, catholic and apostolic Church," and pray for the pope and the local bishop by name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Eucharist, and why Catholics kneel in an empty church. Your line was: he stayed. Who did you stay with a little longer? Day eighteen.

Here's a thing people who travel notice. You can walk into a Catholic Mass in Lagos, in Manila, in a tiny village in Poland, in a strip-mall parish in Texas. The language is different. The music is wildly different: drums, organs, guitars, choirs in five-part harmony. But you'd know where you were in about thirty seconds. The readings, the peace, the table. The same shape, in a language you don't speak. Every Sunday, Catholics around the world say a creed that calls the Church one, holy, catholic and apostolic. Today, the small-c word in that line, which doesn't mean what most people think.
screen: `LAGOS, MANILA, POLAND, TEXAS.` → `THE SAME SHAPE.` → `ONE, HOLY, CATHOLIC.`

segments.voice: Start with church. In the New Testament the Greek word is ekklesia, from a verb meaning to call out. It meant an assembly, people called out of their houses to gather. So the Church, first of all, isn't a building. It's the people who were called. Now the small-c word. Catholic comes from the Greek katholikos, from kath' holou: according to the whole. Universal. Around the year 110, a bishop named Ignatius of Antioch was being taken to Rome under guard, to be executed. On the way he wrote letters to the churches, and in one of them he uses a phrase no one had put in writing before, as far as we know: the catholic Church. He meant the whole Church, everywhere, gathered around Christ. That's the first time the word appears. The creed said at every Sunday Mass, written down in the fourth century, puts four words side by side. One: many countries, one faith. Holy: set apart for God, even though, as day seven reminded us, its people are far from perfect. Catholic: for everyone, everywhere. Apostolic: going back to the apostles. Catholics believe their Church is one family under the pope, the bishop of Rome, successor of Peter. And it's more varied than people think. Most Catholics belong to the Latin Church, but there are also more than twenty Eastern Catholic Churches, with their own liturgies and traditions, united with Rome. Other Christians use these creed words too. Many Protestants and Orthodox Christians say catholic in the creed and mean the whole Church of Christ across every denomination. Everyone who says it means it big. With more than a billion members, it's commonly said that somewhere on Earth a Mass is always going on. Everywhere at once.
screen: `EKKLESIA — THE ONES CALLED OUT.` · `KATHOLIKOS — ACCORDING TO THE WHOLE.` · `IGNATIUS, ON THE ROAD TO ROME.` · `ONE, HOLY, CATHOLIC, APOSTOLIC.` · then, large: `EVERYWHERE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Picture the globe, slowly turning. Somewhere it's morning, and people are walking into a church. Somewhere it's midnight, and someone is praying alone by a candle. Somewhere a baby is being baptized, and somewhere a funeral is ending. Let the picture be as big as it wants to be. You're one person on it, breathing. If you pray, you can pray for all of them at once. The bell holds the time.
The Church. The ekklesia, the people called out, and catholic, meaning according to the whole: universal. Eighteenth word.
Your line: everywhere at once. Today, think of someone far away who's doing the same ordinary thing you are right now: waking up, eating, working. Day eighteen.

19.title: the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship
19.hook: the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship
19.carry: talk to him like a friend
19.tomorrow: the word Francis (the pope) can't stop saying
19.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Saint Teresa of Ávila on October 15; her books on prayer, especially her Life and The Interior Castle, are still widely read, and Carmelite nuns and friars follow the reform she began.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Church: the ones called out, and catholic, meaning universal. Your line was: everywhere at once. Today, one woman in one small Spanish town. Day nineteen.

Here's a confession most people who try to pray would recognize. You sit down to do it. You mean it. And within a minute you're thinking about lunch, or an argument from last week, or whether you locked the car. You feel like a fraud. Now meet a woman in sixteenth-century Spain who admitted, in writing, that for years she found prayer so hard she'd watch the hourglass, waiting for the time to run out. She was a nun. And she became one of the most important teachers of prayer the Catholic Church has ever had. Today, the saint who wrote about prayer like a friendship.
screen: `YOU SIT DOWN TO PRAY.` → `WITHIN A MINUTE: LUNCH.` → `SHE WATCHED THE HOURGLASS.`

segments.voice: Her name was Teresa, from the walled city of Ávila in Spain. She was born in 1515, into a big, lively family, and as a teenager, by her own account, she was more interested in romance novels and nice clothes than holiness. She entered a Carmelite convent at about twenty. And for years, she says in her autobiography, prayer was a struggle. Distracted, dry, going through the motions. Then, in her late thirties, something changed. And the way she described prayer afterward is the reason she's still read. In her book, called her Life, she says that prayer, as she understands it, is nothing else than friendship: spending time often, alone, with the one we know loves us. Not a performance. Not a speech. Time with a friend. She wrote the way she talked: funny, blunt, full of kitchen pictures. She said God walks among the pots and pans. In another book, The Interior Castle, she pictures the soul as a castle made of a single diamond, with many rooms, and God living in the center. Prayer is the door you go in by. She also got a lot done. She founded new convents across Spain, traveling on bad roads in rough carts, arguing with bishops, and working with a young friar we know as John of the Cross. There's a story people love to tell: that after a cart tipped her into a muddy river, she complained to God, if this is how you treat your friends, no wonder you have so few. Nobody knows whether she really said it. But it sounds exactly like someone who talked to God like a friend. In 1970, she became one of the first two women named a Doctor of the Church.
screen: `ÁVILA, 1515. ROMANCE NOVELS.` · `YEARS OF DRY PRAYER.` · `PRAYER IS FRIENDSHIP.` · `A CASTLE WITH MANY ROOMS.` · then, large: `TALK TO HIM LIKE A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit, with no speech to give. Imagine a friend sitting across from you, one who knows you well and likes you anyway. Tell them, silently, one plain thing about your day. Not the polished version. Then just sit together without talking. When your mind wanders, and it will, come back the way you'd turn back to a friend after a distraction. If you pray, you can make that friend God. The bell holds the time.
Teresa of Ávila. The Carmelite nun who struggled with prayer for years, then described it as friendship with the one who loves us. Nineteenth word.
Your line: talk to him like a friend. Today, while you're doing something ordinary, stirring a pot or walking to the car, say one honest sentence inside, the way you'd talk to a friend. Day nineteen.

20.title: the word Francis (the pope) can't stop saying
20.hook: the word Francis (the pope) can't stop saying
20.howItsDone: Catholics practice the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and forgiving injuries, and celebrate Divine Mercy Sunday on the Sunday after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa of Ávila, and prayer as friendship. Your line was: talk to him like a friend. What did you say, stirring the pot? Day twenty.

In 2013, a man from Buenos Aires who used to ride the bus to work became pope and took a name no pope had ever used: Francis, after the rich kid from Assisi you met on day eight. Journalists started counting the words he used most. One kept coming up, in sermons, in interviews, off the cuff to crowds. He called a whole year after it. He titled a book after it. Asked once, early on, to describe himself, he said, in effect: a sinner the Lord has looked upon. Pope Francis led the Church until his death in 2025, and if you had to sum him up in one word, most people would pick the same one. Today, mercy.
screen: `A POPE WHO RODE THE BUS.` → `ONE WORD KEPT COMING UP.` → `A SINNER THE LORD LOOKED UPON.`

segments.voice: The Latin word is misericordia. Take it apart and it's two words: miseri, the wretched, the ones in trouble, and cor, the heart. Mercy is a heart that goes out to someone in misery. Not a verdict. A heart. The Bible's Hebrew has a word for it that comes from the word for a mother's womb, the kind of love you feel for a child you carried. Luke's Gospel puts it at the center of what Jesus asks, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." Pope Francis took his motto from an old sermon by Bede, an English monk, about the day Jesus called Matthew, a tax collector everyone despised. Jesus looked at him, Bede says, with mercy, and chose him. In Latin: miserando atque eligendo. By having mercy, and by choosing. Francis said that was his own story. That's where today's line comes from. Francis kept saying that people who can't show mercy are often people who have never let themselves receive it. You can't give away what you've never been handed. So the first step is to accept it, to let God, or someone, look at you with mercy and choose you anyway, the way Jesus looked at Matthew. That's hard. Most of us are much harder on ourselves than on anyone else. Then it flows outward: forgiving, feeding, visiting, going toward people in trouble. Catholics call these the works of mercy, and remember Francis of Assisi kissing the leper's hand? That's the same heart. Confession from day twelve is the Church's way of saying it out loud: you're forgiven. Start there.
screen: `MISERICORDIA — A HEART FOR THE WRETCHED.` · `BE YE THEREFORE MERCIFUL.` · `BY HAVING MERCY, AND BY CHOOSING.` · `YOU CAN'T GIVE WHAT YOU WERE NEVER HANDED.` · then, large: `START WITH YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Think of one thing you're still angry at yourself about. Something small or something big. Picture someone who loves you looking at it, and at you, without flinching. Not excusing it. Just looking at you with a heart that goes out to you. Breathe slowly, and let yourself be looked at like that. If you pray, you can let that look be God's. The bell holds the time.
Mercy. Misericordia: a heart that goes out to someone in trouble, received first, then given away. Twentieth word.
Your line: start with yourself. Today, the next time you make a mistake, talk to yourself the way you'd talk to a friend who made it. Day twenty.

21.title: the mountain ahead
21.hook: the mountain ahead; the prayers Jesus himself prayed
21.howItsDone: At every Mass a psalm is sung or said between the readings, and priests, religious and many lay Catholics pray the psalms through the day in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy, the word Pope Francis kept saying. Your line was: start with yourself. Were you a little kinder to yourself? Today is the last day of camp one. Day twenty-one.
screen: `START WITH YOURSELF.` → `THE LAST DAY OF CAMP ONE.`

segments.voice: Look back down the hill for a second. Three weeks ago you started with grace, at a kitchen table. Then the sign of the cross. The Mass, in three scenes. Mary. The saints. Francis. Candles. The rosary: its beads, and the Hail Mary. Confession. Sunday. The Our Father. Lent. Easter. The Eucharist. The Church. Teresa. Mercy. Twenty words. That's the vocabulary: the words a Catholic hears every week. Now look up. There's a mountain ahead, and it's made of stories. But first, one more word, and it's the prayer book that Jesus himself grew up praying.
screen: `TWENTY WORDS, DOWN THE HILL.` → `THE WORDS OF EVERY WEEK.` → `A MOUNTAIN MADE OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: The Psalms are a book of one hundred and fifty songs and prayers in the middle of the Bible. The Hebrew name is Tehillim: praises. Our word psalm comes from Greek, a song sung to a plucked string. They were Israel's prayer book and hymnal, and Jesus, a Jewish boy in Nazareth, would have known many of them by heart. Here's what surprises people: they aren't all nice. Some are joyful. Some are furious. Some are people in the dark asking God where he's gone. On the cross, in Matthew's Gospel, Jesus cries out the first line of one of those, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's a psalm. Even in his worst hour he prayed with words he had most likely learned as a child. And in Luke, his last words are from a psalm too: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Here's a detail you'll notice if you look them up in an older Catholic Bible: the numbers are often off by one. The Douay-Rheims follows the ancient Greek and Latin numbering, so the psalm Jesus cried on the cross is Psalm 21 there, and Psalm 22 in most other Bibles. Same words, different count. Catholics still pray them every day. At every Mass there's a psalm, sung back and forth, between the readings; remember scene one. Priests, monks and nuns pray the psalms through the day in what's called the Liturgy of the Hours. The rosary's hundred and fifty Hail Marys have sometimes been called the poor man's psalter, one for each psalm. One hundred and fifty psalms, one for nearly every feeling a person can have. One hundred and fifty doors.
screen: `TEHILLIM — PRAISES.` · `NOT ALL OF THEM NICE.` · `MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?` · `THE NUMBERS ARE OFF BY ONE.` · then, large: `150 DOORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for the end of camp one. A seventy-five-second sit. Ask yourself what you're actually feeling today, honestly. Glad. Tired. Angry. Lost. Grateful. Whatever it is, the Psalms say there's a door for it, and you don't have to clean it up first. Name the feeling in one word. Then breathe with it, not against it. If you pray, you can hand God that one word, just as it is. The bell holds the time.
The Psalms. One hundred and fifty praises, laments and songs, the prayer book Jesus himself prayed. Twenty-first word, and the last of camp one.
Your line: 150 doors. Today, if you can, open a Bible to the middle and read one psalm, any one. Tomorrow, camp two: the stories, starting with two pregnant women. Day twenty-one.
